title: Types, coercion, strict equality and falsy values

videos.script:
Five plus three is eight. {{plus}} Quote the five, and the answer is fifty-three. Swap the plus for a minus, and it is two again.

None of that is a bug. {{types}} Every value in JavaScript has a type, and when an operator meets two values of different types, the language converts one of them without asking. That conversion is called coercion, and it is the reason JavaScript has a reputation.

The reputation is half deserved. {{rules}} The rules are written down and they never change, so once you know the three or four that matter, the surprises stop being surprises.

Today: the seven primitive types, and what typeof says about each. {{numbers}} Why zero point one plus zero point two is not zero point three, and what to do about money. {{convert}} How to turn text into a number on purpose, so the language does not do it for you. {{equality}} Two equals signs against three, and why you will write three. {{falsy}} And the eight values that count as false, which decide what every if statement in your program does.

By the end, a form field that adds ten and five and gets one hundred and five will look like exactly what it is.
